title: Seven Thousand Verses for a City

title_i18n.en: Seven Thousand Verses for a City

subtitle: How Bhoja Turned Stone, Verse, and City into One Science
era: Samarangana Sutradhara and Paramara architectural science, c. 1010-1055 CE
region: Dhara, Bhojpur, and the temple-building world of Malwa
moral: Knowledge becomes powerful when tested against the world.

sources.citation: Bhoja, Samarangana Sutradhara, ed. V.R. Bhat, Gaekwad's Oriental Series, 1966
sources.note: Standard edition of the 83-chapter Sanskrit architectural treatise.
Later architectural text citing the Samarangana Sutradhara as authority.

sources.citation: Adam Hardy, South Asian Studies 31:1 (2015); Adam Hardy, The Temple Architecture of India (2007)
sources.note: Modern cross-check between text, Bhojpur drawings, and Bhumija temple forms.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of a half-built great temple and city plan etched on the ground, Bhoja at the center with palm-leaf manuscript and measuring cord

dialogue.text: In Bhoja’s Malwa, a king’s court set out to bind earth, temple and machine into one science—the seven thousand verses of the Samarangana Sutradhara.

panels.shot: slow push-in from bird’s-eye of Malwa plateau to close view of Dhara’s palace complex

dialogue.text: Dhara, early eleventh century. Under Bhoja’s gaze, Malwa’s capital swells with streets, shrines and markets—its growth no longer a jumble, but a question: can a city be written like a book?

panels.shot: medium close-up of Bhoja seated in a council hall, scrolls and treatises spread before him

dialogue.text: Earlier masters had spoken of houses and temples in scattered sutras, guild rules and regional memory. Bhoja’s court turned these streams toward one aim: a complete science of building.

panels.shot: low, intimate shot of Bhoja dictating to scribes in lamplight

dialogue.text: The treatise that emerged, later called Samarangana Sutradhara, bears Bhoja’s name. Whether from his own hand or his court’s, its voice is royal: it speaks as if a king instructs the master-builder.

panels.shot: wide shot of open ground outside Dhara with Bhoja and architects testing soil

dialogue.text: The text begins at the ground itself: how to choose land, test soil by sight, smell and touch, judge wind, water and slope—before a single brick is laid.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of a city plan traced with cords and pegs on the earth

dialogue.text: Then come towns and forts: grids and mandalas of streets, wards for traders and artisans, placements for markets, wells and temples. A city is drawn first on earth, then raised in stone.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a partially finished house, carpenters and masons at work

dialogue.text: Domestic life, too, is measured: house types for rich and poor, room proportions, courtyards for light and air, thresholds and doorways aligned not by whim, but by rule.

panels.shot: dramatic wide of Bhojpur riverside with massive platform and unfinished lingam, plans etched nearby

dialogue.text: At Bhojpur, near the Betwa, time preserves a rare echo: the ground-drawings and unfinished mass of a colossal temple, where theory and experiment met under Bhoja’s rule.

panels.shot: top-down close-up of carved planning lines on Bhojpur stones with Bhoja’s hand hovering above

dialogue.text: Modern scholars trace these lines and compare them with the Samarangana’s verses on temple plans and superstructures, seeing in Bhojpur an open page of stone beside a page of verse.

panels.shot: wide, slightly low-angle shot of a Bhumija-type temple shikhara rising against the sky

dialogue.text: The text’s temple chapters dwell on soaring shikharas, including the bhumija form—lattices of miniature spires—which later Malwa temples would turn into stone diagrams of rhythm and repetition.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a sculptor’s workshop with images in different stages

dialogue.text: Beyond plans and walls, the Samarangana speaks of images and icons: measures for limbs, poses and expressions, so that the deity’s presence, the dancer’s grace, follow a shared canon.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of painters at work on a shrine wall

dialogue.text: Painting and ornament, too, find place: how to lay out panels on walls, how colors and motifs should support the shrine’s form, so that structure and image speak one language.

panels.shot: low-lit, focused shot of Bhoja and craftsmen examining a mechanical device without revealing details

dialogue.text: In later chapters, the text turns to yantras—mechanical contrivances, even devices said to fly. Yet it withholds full instruction, hinting at marvels while guarding their working.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bhoja dismissing a courtier excitedly gesturing upwards

dialogue.text: Later ages would weave legends of Bhoja’s flying machines. The text itself, and the earth at Bhojpur, stay silent on such claims, speaking instead of measured craft and controlled wonder.

panels.shot: wide shot of Bhoja teaching architects in a hall, with diagrams and models around

dialogue.text: For Bhoja’s court, architecture was not just craft but shastra—rule and reasoning, passed in sutras, tested in stone, and taught to those who would raise the next generation of cities and shrines.

panels.shot: dissolve-style composition showing a palm-leaf of Samarangana beside a later Aparajitaprccha manuscript

dialogue.text: A century later, the Aparajitaprccha would cite the Samarangana as authority. Bhoja’s courtly compilation, once royal instruction, had become a reference for distant builders.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from Bhoja at Bhojpur to a montage of many temples and towns across Malwa

dialogue.text: Today, scholars walk Bhojpur’s plans and Malwa’s bhumija towers with the Samarangana in hand, tracing how verses shaped stone, and how a king’s curiosity met the test of the world.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Bhoja’s thoughtful face, city and temple blurred behind

dialogue.text: In Bhoja’s age, knowledge proved itself not in boasts but in buildings. His seven thousand verses endure where they were tested—in foundations that still hold, and forms that still rise against the sky.
